title: Why TTS Models Now Look Like LLMs — Samuel Humeau, Mistral
talk_summary: A Mistral scientist explains the architecture of modern text-to-speech models: autoregressive LLM-style backbones over compressed audio tokens, with a small per-frame decoder, and streaming the first audio packets to cut perceived latency. The talk is mostly academic TTS internals with a short discussion of streaming text into speech for voice agents.

takeaways.technique: Stream partial output to start downstream work early
takeaways.what_they_do: They emit the first audio packets as soon as they exist and play them while the rest is still being computed, so perceived latency drops even though total compute time is unchanged.
takeaways.evidence_quote: as soon as you have the first token of the LLM uh the the machine starts to speak
takeaways.numbers: 17 ms from text input to first playable audio on a single GPU (network excluded)

takeaways.technique: Big backbone + small fast decoder split
takeaways.what_they_do: One step of a large backbone per frame, then a small transformer (or diffusion model) expands all tokens of that frame, keeping quality while cutting compute.
takeaways.evidence_quote: having one step of the backbone per frame and a smaller model here uh typically a dev transformer
takeaways.numbers: 4B-parameter backbone; 37 tokens per 80 ms frame; ~500 tokens/sec
